title: Not So Innocent: Toddlers' Inferences About Costs and Culpability

selection.evidence: Assigned by mark as item 1 of 8 in a blinded known-answer control of my reading protocol (identifiers only, 2026-10-23T16:11). No prior knowledge of the paper; prior suspicion: none.

cost.compute_notes: Published PDF (author copy, Yale lab page; SAGE is behind a Cloudflare wall) read in full. OSF z9ikh (CSV + R), frwun and 4qfvj (materials, 19 MB demo video) acquired with checksums. Authors' AnalyzeData.R run unmodified in Docker image zoo-r-psych:4.4.1 (rocker/r-ver 4.4.1 + CRAN binaries); the two 500,000-replicate difference bootstraps through dplyr::filter are the slow step. Python recount, exact tests and a 4,000-simulation known-answer study of the bootstrap.

triggers: do toddlers infer culpability from the cost of an action
naive utility calculus children moral judgment
known-answer control psychological science 2015 open data

claims.statement: Toddlers (mean 21.6 months) prefer an agent who achieves a goal at lower cost: 15 of 16 chose the competent puppet (Exp 1).
claims.scope: Exp 1, n = 16 analysed of 24 tested (5 excluded by coder, 3 no choice).

our_assessment.why: Recounted exactly from the deposit; strong against chance. The published CI [87.5%, 100%] is the R 'basic' interval truncated: R prints (0.8750, 1.0625); the truncation is not stated.

claims.statement: When both agents refuse to help, 2-year-olds still prefer to play with the competent agent (Exp 2: 11/16; Exp 3 play: 13/16).
claims.scope: Exp 2 and Exp 3 play condition, n = 16 each.

quantities.name: exp2_chose_competent
quantities.baseline: binomial p = 0.21 (paper: 'a bias toward the competent agent')

quantities.name: exp3_play_chose_competent
quantities.baseline: binomial p = 0.021; published CI lower bound 68.75% is a typo, the authors' script, figure code and R output all give 62.50%

our_assessment.why: Holds pooled (24/32, p = .007) and in Exp 3 alone; Exp 2 alone (11/16, p = .21) is not distinguishable from chance and the paper calls it 'a bias'. Exp 3's play CI is misprinted.

claims.statement: When both agents refuse to help, children infer that the less competent agent is nicer (abstract); the shift relative to a no-refusal baseline is reported as 'a decrease of 37.5% (95% CI = [6.17%, 71.03%]; p < .075, Fisher exact test)'.
claims.scope: Exp 3 nicer vs nicer-baseline (same 'which one is nicer?' question; refusal vs none), n = 16 each.

quantities.name: fisher_two_sided_nicer_vs_baseline
quantities.baseline: paper prints 'p < .075' -- false; the authors' own script prints p-value = 0.0756

quantities.name: boschloo_two_sided_nicer_vs_baseline
quantities.baseline: Barnard 0.0502; Fisher rejects only 1.6-1.8% under the null at this n (r02)

quantities.name: fisher_power_at_observed_effect_11v5_n16
quantities.baseline: exact enumeration; the paper says it 'predicted strong effect sizes' and set n = 16

our_assessment.why: The single cell supporting the claim is 11/16 (p = .21 vs chance). Against its proper control the evidence sits on the threshold under every reasonable test (Fisher .0756, Boschloo .0501). The paper prints the Fisher p as 'p < .075', which is false. The stronger comparison (play vs nicer, Fisher p = .011) changes the question asked, so it cannot isolate an inference about niceness from a preference to play. Bounds over the 8 non-responders move the decisive p from .004 to .545. Reproducible, honestly deposited, over-stated in the abstract.

claims.statement: The authors' non-stratified 'basic' bootstrap CI for a difference of two proportions is only mildly liberal at n = 16 per group: under a true null it excludes 0 in 5.7-6.9% of 4,000 simulated studies (p = .5, .3125, .6875), while Fisher's exact test rejects in 1.6-1.8%. The gap between the paper's CI (excludes 0) and its Fisher p (.0756) is mostly Fisher's conservatism, not a broken interval.
claims.scope: Simulation, n = 16 per group, B = 2,000 per simulated study; Python re-implementation of boot(type='basic') with row resampling of the pooled 32 (what the authors' code does).

our_assessment.why: Known-answer simulation with the null forced in; the same harness detects the forced 11/16 vs 5/16 effect 61% (bootstrap) / 44% (Fisher) of the time.

checked.how: Read tool on the PDF, pages 1-8
checked.result: Primary source. journals.sagepub.com returns a Cloudflare 'Just a moment...' page to curl. Supplemental Material (adult survey) not retrieved.

137 rows, classic-Mac CR line endings (no LF). Every N, exclusion reason, choice count and age statistic in the paper recounts exactly. One exact duplicate row (Exp 3 control, F, 768 days, Competent, D/C/D): twins or a copy; removing it leaves the decisive p at 0.0756.

checked.how: MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 docker run --rm -v "<osf_z9ikh/files/osfstorage>:/data:ro" -w /tmp zoo-r-psych:4.4.1 bash -c 'cp /data/* /tmp/ && Rscript AnalyzeData.R'
checked.result: Runs unmodified in R 4.4.1. Output in reanalysis/out/authors_AnalyzeData_R_run.txt: Exp1 basic CI (0.875, 1.0625), play (0.625, 1.000), Fisher play-vs-nicer 0.01134, Fisher nicer-vs-control 0.0756. The play-vs-nicer difference bootstrap is unseeded: this run gave (0.2143, 0.8125) vs published [21.05%, 81.67%]. The seeded nicer-vs-control bootstrap (set.seed(59283)) gives (0.0617, 0.7095) vs published [6.17%, 71.03%]: the upper bound differs even with the seed, consistent with R 3.6's change of sample()'s default (sample.kind 'Rejection'); my Python re-implementation gives 70.95, matching current R.

open_questions: Unblinding (mark, known_answer_control): was this paper among the third-party-established 'sound' ones? My call before unblinding: data and analysis reproducible; checked-type defects minor (a mistyped CI bound, a false 'p < .075', an unstated truncation); central claim over-stated.

Is non-response informative here? 5/21 in the nicer condition made no choice vs 2/18 (play) and 3/19 (baseline). A replication that records why children did not answer would settle whether the 'nicer' judgement survives intention-to-treat.
